hypothesis.title: The Coherence Contract
hypothesis.question: When a musical sketch changes surface material, which invariant best predicts whether listeners still hear the layers as belonging together: harmonic graph adjacency, perceptual band separation, phase/microtiming relation, or call-and-response timing?
hypothesis.hypothesis: If a call-and-response sketch preserves one explicit coherence contract while varying surface details, then listeners will tolerate larger changes than they will in a version that keeps more surface material but breaks the chosen invariant.
hypothesis.rationaleMd: S1 frames harmonic resources as graph/configuration relations, so harmonic coherence can be operationalized as path adjacency rather than chord-name sameness. S3 suggests spectral organization can be made perceptually meaningful by aligning processing bands to Bark-scale critical bands rather than arbitrary crossovers. S5 argues that pitch and phase equivariance improve stem retrieval and better track human musical-coherence judgments than phase-discarding baselines. S2 adds that multi-scale representations need the right temporal and frequency grain to remain stable without losing fine acoustic distinctions. S4 warns that encoder/compression choices determine what acoustic information survives degradation, and S6 supplies a studio-facing structure where call, response, contrast, and silence carry musical continuity. Together these sources support testing coherence as an explicit invariant contract rather than as generic similarity.

recipe.title: Coherence Under Surface Change
recipe.bodyMd: Create a 60-second call-and-response sketch with a four-note lead call, a bass/chord answer, and a quiet binding layer. Render four versions. Version A varies answer chords only by a chosen Tonnetz-adjacent rule [S1]. Version B keeps the harmonic path but moves timbres into cleaner perceptual bands inspired by Bark-scale critical-band thinking [S3]. Version C keeps notes and timbre stable while varying phase/microtiming between answer and binding layer [S5]. Version D deliberately breaches one contract: a non-adjacent harmonic answer, masking in the same critical band, phase smear, or silence inserted where response continuity is expected [S4, S6]. The test is falsified if the breach version is rated as equally coherent as the contract-preserving versions despite listeners noticing the manipulation.

parameters.value: 8-bar call-and-response loop repeated with four treatments

dawChecklist: Program a four-note lead call and a bass/chord answer at 112 BPM.
Add a quiet rhythmic or textural binding layer with a stable phase/timing relationship to the answer.
Render Version A: vary answer harmony only by the selected graph-adjacent rule.
Render Version B: preserve harmony but separate call and answer into perceptually clearer frequency bands.
Render Version C: preserve pitch and timbre but vary phase/microtiming between answer and binding layer.
Render Version D: deliberately break one contract while leaving much surface material intact.
Blind-listen without viewing the session and rate coherence 1-5 for each render.
Note which invariant carried coherence: graph path, band placement, phase/timing, or call-response silence.

protocol.listeningContext: DAW bounce or playlist, eyes off the arrangement view, same playback level for all renders.
protocol.listeningMethod: Blind shuffle the four renders, rate coherence 1-5, then identify the perceived reason each version held together or broke.
whatVaries: harmonic graph adjacency in Version A
perceptual band placement in Version B
one deliberate contract breach in Version D

notes: This synthesis deliberately frames coherence as an invariant contract, distinct from prior identity-budget and boundary/carrier framings.
